children.text: The first thing to decide for a family trip in Egypt is not the hotel name. Is it a sea-and-rest trip or a sites trip? Are the children small, or old enough to respond to history? The answer decides the region.
There are three main shapes of family travel in Egypt. One is a Red Sea resort stay —
Hurghada
, Makadi Bay,
Marsa Alam
. Another is the Sinai, where Sharm el-Sheikh is centred on the sea and snorkelling. The third combines
Cairo
Luxor
, and
Aswan
to put children inside actual ancient Egypt.

Inside the same "Egypt trip," these three are quite different in substance. With small children, where you prize daily meals, naps, the pool, and short transfers, an all-inclusive on the Red Sea is a strong option. With children who can swim and respond to the underwater world, Sharm works well. With children eight and older who can engage with pyramids, mummies, and temples, the value of Cairo and Luxor goes up sharply.
So there is no single best family resort. The answer turns on the family's ages, stamina, interests, and how much itinerary the parents want to build.
Hurghada: easy sea for small children

Hurghada is the most legible Red Sea choice for families. Many hotels are close to the airport, and what a family trip needs — all-inclusive, pool, kids' club, beach, evening shows — generally completes inside the property.

This is not a place to expect strong city appeal. Hurghada's advantage is not urban tourism; it is the ease of staying inside the hotel. For families with younger children, "not having to move" is large. Breakfast, pool, nap, beach, an early dinner. You can keep that rhythm without breaking it.

Steigenberger-style resorts, Rixos properties, and Pickalbatros aquapark-style hotels are familiar candidates here. For upper-end taste, look at service consistency and room size; for waterslide focus, look at aquapark scale; for ease of food, look at the all-inclusive content.

What to watch in Hurghada is that hotels vary a lot. Even within "family-friendly," a property can lean toward toddlers, toward teenagers, toward pool, or toward beach, and the experience changes. Before booking, check recent reviews for the kids' club, pool safety, food, and ease of getting onto the beach.
Makadi Bay: for families that settle into the resort

Makadi Bay is the resort area south of Hurghada. It sits a little away from the busier centre and suits a more inside-the-resort stay. Hotels with large pools, water parks, and big grounds make it easier for children to spend an entire day on site without getting bored.

The trade-off is that the airport transfer is a little longer than central Hurghada. The premise is to spend time inside the hotel rather than going out for meals or walks. If that is easier for the family, Makadi Bay is a good choice. For a family that wants a different town walk each evening, it can feel closed.
If you pick Makadi Bay, the inside of the hotel essentially is the trip. Look carefully at room size, pool, slides, children's programmes, and food choices.
Sharm el-Sheikh: strong for swimming children
Sharm el-Sheikh's appeal is the sea itself. Reef, clarity,
Ras Mohammed National Park
, boat trips out toward the Strait of Tiran. For families interested in snorkelling and diving, Sharm can leave a stronger impression than Hurghada.
Smaller children need some care. Many Sharm beaches are not gentle walk-in sand; some entries use jetties or reef edges. For children who can't yet swim, the sea's appeal may not be fully usable.

The Four Seasons Resort Sharm el-Sheikh is an upper-end option for families who prize service quality, rooms, and family programmes. Public information lists the Kids For All Seasons programme for ages 4 to 12 alongside other family facilities. Rixos Premium Seagate suits families who prize all-inclusive, water parks, and the Rixy Kids Club.
In Sharm, the position of the hotel's bay matters. Near
Naama Bay
, dining out and boat departures are convenient. The Nabq side is quieter and more resort-like, but further from the centre. Choose by bay and stay style, not by brand alone.
Cairo: not a resort, but the core of a family trip

Cairo is not a typical family resort destination. For an Egypt family trip, however, there is no need to skip it. If children have any knowledge of ancient Egypt from school or books, the combination of the
Giza
pyramids and the Grand Egyptian Museum is a very strong experience.

For lodging in Cairo, decide by purpose. If the centre of the trip is the pyramids and the GEM, a hotel on the Giza side is convenient. The Marriott Mena House — where the view of the pyramid is itself part of the stay — leaves a particularly clear impression on children.
If you want to see Islamic Cairo,
Coptic Cairo

, the Nile, and restaurants, central Cairo or Nile-side hotels become candidates. Cairo is heavy with traffic, however. For family travel, a plan that does not push long transfers every day is important.
Cairo is not a place to use as "easy resort rest." It is a place for building strong days. Don't overload the pyramids and the museum; build in hotel rest time, and the trip works.
Luxor: where older children gain the most
Luxor is a place that deserves more family attention than it usually gets in Egypt. The
Valley of the Kings
, Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple. These are not textbook illustrations; they are places where you feel size in the body.
It is not for very young children. Heat, distances, the size of the sites, the volume of explanation — these suit children of eight or older, and ideally those who can engage with history a little.

For families in Luxor, a Nile-side hotel with a pool is easy to use. A property like the Hilton Luxor Resort & Spa sits close to Karnak, with pool and Nile views, and works as the place to rest after sites. The point is to use the hotel as the rest device for sightseeing.
In Luxor, see sites early in the morning, rest at midday, and go out again in the late afternoon. Pushing through the midday tires adults and children both.
All-inclusive or breakfast-only
On the Red Sea, all-inclusive often suits families. Children want drinks and snacks repeatedly, and going out for meals adds transfer load — all-inclusive lets you read both cost and effort.
In Cairo and Luxor, all-inclusive is not necessarily right. Breakfast-only is usually enough. You go out for sites in the day and fit lunch and dinner to the itinerary.
Don't conflate the two cases. At a sea resort, the hotel is the centre of the trip. In Cairo or Luxor, the hotel is the base that supports the trip.
By age
Under six, prioritise short transfers, shallow pools, kids' menus, and easy naps. Large resorts in Hurghada or Makadi Bay fit.
Seven to eleven, combine Red Sea time and a light sites experience. Sharm for snorkelling, or a short Cairo segment added to a Hurghada stay.
Twelve and up, the value of Cairo and Luxor rises sharply. Ancient Egypt, mummies, royal tombs, temples, the geography of the Nile become understandable as a concrete world, not just "hot ruins."
Season

October through April is the easiest for family travel. The Red Sea is comfortable, and Cairo and Luxor are less severe than midsummer. December and January are popular and prices climb. Spring break and European school holidays also crowd.
Summer prices drop, but the heat of Luxor and Cairo is hard on family travel. A Red Sea–only trip works; a sites-heavy trip in summer does not.
Finally
An Egypt family trip can end at the resort, and the warm sea, the pool, and the all-inclusive comfort can make a perfectly enjoyable trip.

What Egypt actually offers families, however, is the chance to put "moments where the world widens" inside a holiday. Standing in front of a pyramid. Looking at Tutankhamun's funerary equipment. Walking between the columns at Karnak. Swimming over real reef on the Red Sea.

A good family hotel is the place that supports those experiences. It rests the children, doesn't exhaust the parents, and brings everyone back to a state where they can actually enjoy the next day of Egypt. That is the most important criterion when choosing family lodging here.

deck: Choosing family lodging in Egypt starts with sea vs. sites, the children's ages, and how much travel they can carry. A practical look at Hurghada, Sharm, Cairo, and Luxor from a family's point of view.
